A documented family history

Two family lines,
kept in one record.

This is the ancestry Nolan and Norah inherit through both parents: Robin’s Cymbalista–Johnson line and April’s Israel–Parajas–Apostol line.

It distinguishes records from family reconstruction, and historical setting from personal fact. Uncertainty is preserved because an honest question is more useful than a confident mistake.

Editor’s note

What changed in this edition

April is correctly recorded as Robin’s former wife and the mother of Nolan and Norah—not as Robin’s sibling. Her ancestry is restored from the supplied seven-page family chart.

Robin married Adi on 22 August 2026. Robin and Adi have no children together. Living people are named only where the relationship is necessary; their portraits, birth dates, and locations remain private.

AJHS + first-hand eulogy

Documentary chapters

What is distinctive about this family past

These are not sales points. They are the recurring patterns that make the evidence worth preserving for the next generation.

01

A name that remembers music

Cymbalista is understood as an occupational name associated with the cimbalom, a hammered-string instrument of Central and Eastern Europe. The narrative remembers Wolf and Icyk as musicians. The surname meaning is credible context; their personal occupations remain unverified.

02

A teacher’s reputation crossed borders

Rachmil is remembered as a rabbi, but the supplied gravestone summary more specifically emphasizes Torah teaching. That distinction matters: the strongest surviving religious inheritance may be learning and transmission rather than formal office.

03

Migration changed spelling, work, and memory

Przysucha became Warsaw; Warsaw became London; London opened into Boston, Sydney, and São Paulo. Simblist, Cymbalist, Symberlist, and eventually Johnson show how migration altered public identity while family relationships remained underneath.

04

A lost Jewish connection was reconstructed

The Johnson descendants reportedly grew up without knowing the Warsaw Jewish connection. Family research argues that DNA matches and records restored that link roughly a century later. It is a compelling reconstruction, but the match-by-match evidence should be published privately for review.

05

The children inherit a second migration history

April’s chart adds a Filipino story centered on the Israel, Parajas, and Apostol families. Pangasinan is the leading geographic clue, not yet a proven town-by-town route. This branch brings its own surnames, possible parish records, and traditions that deserve direct oral-history interviews.

Faith, religion, and tradition

What can be inherited—and what still needs asking

Religious context belongs in the record, but it must not be mistaken for proof about a particular person.

Jewish learning

Hebrew names, reported Torah teaching, synagogue service, Jewish burial, and memorial naming form the clearest Jewish thread. Samuel Simblist’s public Jewish life in Sydney is independently documented.

Mixed evidence

Przysucha and Hasidism

Przysucha became a major center of Polish Hasidism associated with the Holy Jew and Simcha Bunim. That makes it essential context, but there is no evidence yet that this family followed the Przysucha court.

Context only

April’s family traditions

Roman Catholicism is historically prominent in Pangasinan and the wider Ilocos Region, and the Diocese of Lingayen-Dagupan has extensive parish registers. Neither fact proves what April’s parents or grandparents practiced.

Ask the family

Questions for oral history

Which holidays were observed? Which prayers, foods, languages, saints, synagogue or parish communities mattered? Which customs continued after migration? Answers should be attributed to the person who remembers them.

Interview priority
For Nolan and Norah

Your roots include Jewish communities in Poland, England, America, and Australia, and Filipino family lines that point toward Pangasinan. These places can help you understand your ancestors, but they do not decide what you must believe.

Corrections and additions

A family source of truth must remain revisable

Proposed changes should identify one claim, preserve the earlier wording, attach or describe evidence, and appear in a dated revision note after review.

Useful submissions

  • The person and exact claim being changed.
  • A record link, photograph, inscription, or attributed first-hand account.
  • Who supplied it and whether it may be public.

Review sequence

  1. Preserve the existing claim.
  2. Attach proposed evidence.
  3. Review contradictions and privacy.
  4. Publish a dated revision note.

Priority questions

  • Which Pangasinan municipality was Benjamin born in?
  • What faith and holiday traditions did April’s family practice?
  • Can the Cymbalista grave inscriptions be re-photographed?
  • Can the DNA chain be documented match by match?
Propose a correction or addition

GitHub submissions are public. Do not attach unredacted records or photographs of living people; describe private evidence and arrange a secure review instead.
